paragraphs: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai. Dasi — Dasai — Dosai.

In Ketubot 111b, Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai says: "From Lod to Ono is three mil; I started out early at twilight and walked up to my ankles in fig honey" (and the reading of Seder HaDorot is "ben Dosai"). And in Yerushalmi Shabbat ch. 7 halakhah 1 (25a) and Bava Batra ch. 2 halakhah 9 he is mentioned under the name Rabbi Yaakov ben Dosai; in Makkot ch. 1 halakhah 7 under the name Rabbi Yaakov bar Dasi; and in Sanhedrin beginning of ch. 4 under the name Rabbi Yaakov bar Dasayi.

And in the Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon, printed in Seder HaChachamim part 1, ch. 4, item 21, it says that Rabbi Yaakov ben Dosai was in the time of Rabbi Meir, and Hyman calls this a scribal error. The error came from Yerushalmi Sanhedrin ch. 2, halakhah 1, which says there: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dasai discusses the point of difference between them — Rabbi Meir used to say ... Rabbi Yehudah says ... . But Hyman takes the plain meaning to be that Rabbi Yaakov ben Dosai was explaining that whether one interrupts [the Temple service] is the point of difference between them, as Pnei Moshe explains there.

notes.text: Neshef means twilight and does not by itself settle morning versus evening. Mil is the Talmudic distance unit. The fig-honey account occurs in the checked William Davidson text at Ketubot 111b; the notice gives 111a.

Pnei Moshe explains the point of difference as whether the high priest interrupts the Temple service. His gloss compares Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon, while Hyman’s condensed citation mentions Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah. Hyman’s chronological objection to the Epistle remains his argument.

The directly consulted Penei Moshe on Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 2:1 explains interruption during the Temple service and compares Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Shimon, then discusses Rabbi Yehudah. Hyman’s compressed wording is retained. His Epistle chronology objection remains his argument, without claiming independent inspection of its exact printed edition.
